issues.legal_issue: A remand should be confined to an identifiable issue overlooked by the lower appellate court when the remaining findings have been concurrently decided and need no reopening.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of rented premises for the personal occupation of one of the owners.
The trial court and first appellate court both found that the premises were required for personal occupation and that the balance of hardship favoured the landlord.
During the appeal, the tenant offered to surrender one room, but the first appellate court did not consider the offer.
The High Court set aside the first appellate court’s judgment and remanded the appeal generally.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s judgment was set aside, but the remand was retained only for consideration of the overlooked offer and the related questions of whether the premises could be conveniently divided and whether the offer would meet the landlord’s need. Findings on all other questions were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: In the context of an eviction claim under Sections 13(1)(g) and 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, where a specific issue was not considered, a finding may be called for on that issue or the remand limited to it; the entire appeal need not be reopened. The Court referred to Article 227 of the Constitution in describing the High Court proceeding and relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a tenant eviction dispute.
predicates.concurrent_findings_on_other_issues: The trial court and the first appellate court have reached the same findings on issues other than the overlooked issue.
predicates.lower_court_overlooked_identifiable_issu: The lower court failed to consider a specific issue that can be addressed separately.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal contains concurrent findings on other matters and a specific issue was overlooked, the remand is confined to that issue.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s offer to surrender part of rented premises requires assessment of whether the premises can be conveniently divided and, if so, whether the offered part meets the landlord’s established need.
material_facts: The landlord’s claim for possession rested on the personal need of one of the owners, and the lower courts had found in the landlord’s favour on that need.
While the appeal was pending, the tenant offered to surrender one of the three rooms in his occupation.
The first appellate court did not consider the offer.
The landlord already had use of a hall in the building.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court was directed to decide whether the premises could be conveniently split up. If they could not, the suit was to succeed; if they could, the court was to determine whether the tenant’s offer adequately met the owner’s need.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, possession may be recovered where premises are reasonably and bona fide required for the landlord’s occupation or that of a person for whose benefit they are held; Section 13(2) restricts eviction where greater hardship would result from granting possession. In this case, the Court directed that a partial-possession offer be assessed first for convenient divisibility and, only if division was possible, for adequacy in meeting the established need. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.tenant_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a tenant eviction dispute.
predicates.landlord_need_established: The lower courts have found that the landlord has a genuine need for the rented premises.
predicates.tenant_offers_partial_possession: The tenant offers to surrender only part of the rented premises.

issues.definition: In a tenant eviction appeal where the landlord’s need has been established and the tenant offers only part of the premises, the court determines whether division is convenient and, if it is, whether the offered part meets that need.
